title: Pre-Procedure GLP-1 Readiness for Endoscopy and Ortho
one_liner: A 7-day workflow plus day-of gastric ultrasound that stops GLP-1 patients from being cancelled or aspirating at surgery centers.
customer: GI endoscopy centers, orthopedic groups, ASCs and their anesthesia groups.
problem: ASA reversed course in Oct 2024 and now advises most patients to continue GLP-1s, shifting the risk to residual gastric contents on the day. Centers cancel or abort cases, and 38% of GLP-1 users vs 8% of non-users were malnourished before joint surgery, which raises complication risk. There is no standard workflow, so every center improvises.
solution: Automated intake (drug, dose, indication, GI symptoms), tailored liquid-diet and hold instructions aligned to multi-society guidance, a malnutrition screen with a protein prehab plan, and nurse-performed gastric POCUS with AI-assisted antral grading and documentation on the day. Priced per case.
why_now: With ~22% of households containing a user, this is routine, not exceptional. Gastric POCUS studies are appearing (2025-26) and centers are looking for a defensible protocol after the 2024 guideline change.
revenue_model: $60-150 per GLP-1 patient case, plus anesthesia-group license and ultrasound rental.
non_obvious_insight: Centers will not stop scheduling GLP-1 patients, so the value is avoided same-day cancellations (thousands of dollars each) and defensible documentation. The buyer is the center's operations and anesthesia leadership, not the drug companies.
first_30_days: Sell to one endoscopy center and one anesthesia group. Supply paper-plus-SMS intake, protocols, a rented handheld ultrasound and training. Track cancellation rate before and after and price at $75 per case.

title: Robot Basecoating for Tabletop Miniature Armies
one_liner: A batch service where vision-guided robot airbrush cells prime, zenithal-shade and basecoat plastic miniatures so hobbyists only paint the details.
customer: Tabletop wargamers with unpainted backlogs, tournament players who need painted armies, and commission-painter studios who subcontract the tedious stages.
problem: An army is 100+ models, and priming and basecoating are the tedious first 60% of the work. Commission painters charge $10-60 per model and take months. Games Workshop's FY2026 revenue of GBP 626.8M shows the scale of the hobby.
solution: Customers ship assembled models. A low-cost robot arm learned from expert airbrushers primes, zenithal-shades and single-color basecoats. Humans QA and finish edges, and the army returns in about 10 days. Start human-in-the-loop with teleoperation and automate progressively.
why_now: Low-cost open-source robot arms and imitation-learning policies matured in 2025. A search for a commercial robot-airbrush painting service for miniatures found none.
revenue_model: $1.50-4 per model, $99-399 per army, and a subscription 'paint club' for batches.
non_obvious_insight: The community fetishizes painting but dislikes the first stage. The robot needs consistency, not artistry, on surfaces that hidden under detail work. Human painters keep the premium layer and become customers and distribution.
first_30_days: Hand-airbrush 50 armies to validate price and turnaround through r/Warhammer and local clubs. Build a teleop rig with a ~$3k arm and airbrush. Ship the first 20 orders.

title: Unstaffed Overnight ICU for Vet Clinics
one_liner: Radar-based contactless vitals and camera analytics let general practices keep IV-fluid and post-op patients overnight without a 24-hour staff, easing ER transfers and ER overload.
customer: 2-10 DVM general practices and low-cost clinics with a small treatment ward, plus shelter medical wards such as parvo units.
problem: With about 2 techs per vet, most clinics cannot staff nights, so hospitalized pets are transferred to 24-hour ERs at higher cost, sent home early or not treated. That drives owner cost, client loss and ER crowding.
solution: A low-cost mmWave radar puck per cage measures respiratory rate and motion, with a camera to watch IV lines and pumps. An on-site alert plus a pooled remote overnight RVT/DVM desk cover 20 clinics, with thresholds tuned by species and weight.
why_now: Consumer sleep-tracking made mmWave sensors cheap, edge vision models run on small devices, the tech shortage is structural, and the spectrum-of-care movement wants intermediate options between full transfer and no treatment.
revenue_model: $150 per cage hardware plus $79-149 per cage per month, and per-night remote-coverage fees.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone tries to automate diagnosis. The binding constraint is night hours: the lack of an awake person forces a general practice to hand revenue and clients to the ER. Monitoring substitutes for staying awake, not for the doctor.
first_30_days: Buy off-the-shelf radar and cameras and instrument 4 cages in 2 friendly clinics. Log respiratory-rate accuracy against manual counts for 30 nights. Sell $99-per-cage pilots and recruit pooled overnight RVT coverage.

title: Battery passport starter that feeds on repair-shop events
one_liner: A cheap battery-passport package for e-bike and small pack makers, plus a repair-shop scanning app that supplies the lifecycle events the passport is legally supposed to track.
customer: Small and mid-size European e-bike, e-scooter and cargo-bike brands, pack assemblers, and industrial or storage battery integrators above 2 kWh. The battery passport must exist from 18 Feb 2027. Independent repair shops and refurbishers are the second user group.
problem: From 18 Feb 2027, LMT, EV and industrial batteries over 2 kWh need a passport reachable by QR code and linked to a unique identifier. The Annex XIII list has 71 entries, but 'not every field is due in February 2027': fields are day-one, modelled-now-populated-later, or waiting on secondary legislation. Access-rights rules are slipping to Q4 2026 and key standards are still in draft. Passports must track state of health, cycle counts and status changes after repurposing or remanufacturing. As one guide says, 'a once-published PDF or marketing microsite is not enough'. Enterprise passport platforms are priced for large firms with compliance teams.
solution: Two products. (1) A brand starter package: a field-status mapper that says which of the 71 fields are due now, later or pending; ISO/IEC 15459-style unique ID and QR generation; a hosted passport page; and a written-authorisation template so the brand can legally delegate passport management to us. (2) A free repair-shop and refurbisher app that scans the QR, logs state-of-health tests, cell swaps, cycle data and second-life events, and pushes them into the brand's passport. Shops get a free workflow tool and repair leads. Brands pay for the passport and the event stream. This also lines up with the replaceable-battery rule that applies from 18 Feb 2027 and with the Right to Repair Directive.
why_now: The passport deadline is under 5 months away and the access-rights implementing act is late. Replaceable portable batteries and e-bike batteries become an obligation on the same date. Eighteen Member States had not notified full transposition of the Right to Repair Directive by September 2026, which leaves national repair rules unsettled while shops still have to service batteries.
revenue_model: Brand setup of EUR 2-5k. Subscription of roughly EUR 1-3 per battery per year (or a EUR 300-1,500 per month floor). Optional per-event fee for verified state-of-health tests. Later, a paid API for insurers and second-life buyers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone sells 'publish a QR page'. The law's real burden is a lifecycle record kept consistent across systems and updated when the battery is serviced or repurposed, and that happens in repair shops that no passport vendor serves. Evidence: 'The hard part is not publishing a page. The hard part is keeping model-level, plant-level, and individual-battery records consistent', passports must track state of health, cycle counts and status changes, and batteries allow the operator to authorise another actor in writing to manage the passport (https://infodpp.eu/en/blog/battery-dpp-deadline-february-2027/). Mid-scale companies are named as the likely pressure point (https://www.batterytechonline.com/design-manufacturing/preparing-for-eu-battery-qr-code-standards-in-2027) and passport software is described as badly priced for small manufacturers (https://dpp-tool.com/en/guide/dpp-software-comparison/). Replaceability and spare-battery availability from 18 Feb 2027 are covered at https://www.intertek.com/blog/2025/06-27-2027-reqs-for-removability-and-replaceability-of-batteries-in-electrical-products/. Right to Repair transposition gap: https://www.eunews.it/en/2026/09/25/right-to-repair-italy-and-17-other-countries-have-failed-to-transpose-the-directive-eu-infringement-proceedings-begin/.
first_30_days: Build a spreadsheet-based field-status mapper for the 71 fields and offer it as a free download. Contact 30 small e-bike brands and pack assemblers found through European trade fairs, cycling industry associations and importer lists. Sell 3 paid 'passport readiness sprint' engagements at EUR 1.5-3k each that end with a hosted pilot passport for one battery model. In parallel, recruit 10 independent e-bike shops to test the scan-and-log app on real service jobs.

title: Fixed-Price MDR Clinical Evaluation Reports via ASReview
one_liner: A tech-enabled service that uses the open-source ASReview active-learning screener plus medical writers to deliver audit-ready literature-based Clinical Evaluation Reports at a fraction of consultant prices.
customer: EU MDR device makers with 5-50 staff: digital-health and software-as-a-medical-device startups, legacy Class I/IIa/IIb device makers, and regulatory consultants who need white-label capacity.
problem: MDR requires a Clinical Evaluation Report built on a systematic literature review with appraisal, state-of-the-art analysis and ongoing updates. Consultants charge roughly EUR 10-40k for a literature-based CER. Small firms delay certification or withdraw legacy products because of clinical-evaluation cost.
solution: Run the search protocol in PubMed and other open sources, ClinicalTrials.gov and vigilance databases. Screen with ASReview LAB (validated in Nature Machine Intelligence) with the full screening log retained. A medical writer and a clinical expert appraise and sign off. Deliver the CER plus a PRISMA-style flow diagram and search-string appendix, then sell a quarterly 'living' update for post-market clinical follow-up.
why_now: Legacy-device MDR transition deadlines fall in 2027-2028 and notified-body capacity is tight. Half of medtechs report expecting to spend 5% or more of revenue on MDR. ASReview is mature and widely used in academia, but no one packages it for regulatory work.
revenue_model: Fixed fee of EUR 4-9k per literature-based CER on low-risk devices. Recurring literature-update subscriptions of EUR 1.2-3k per year. Wholesale white-label pricing for consultancies.
non_obvious_insight: Notified bodies rarely reject a CER because the science is thin. They reject it because the methodology is undocumented: search protocol, appraisal criteria, equivalence reasoning. ASReview's transparent, reproducible logging is the compliance artifact, so sell reproducibility rather than speed.
first_30_days: Recruit two freelance medical writers and one clinician-reviewer. Publish three sample CER sections for a public device category as proof. Post in regulatory-affairs communities (RAPS chapters, MDR LinkedIn groups). Sell the first five CERs at a design-partner price and use the audit trail from each as the case study.

title: Agent-Bookable Gateway for Local Trades
one_liner: A per-business endpoint that lets consumers' AI agents get a photo-based quote, hold a slot and pay a deposit at a local trade without a phone call.
customer: House cleaners, junk-removal crews, pressure washers, mobile detailers, movers, handymen and groomers (1-15 staff) with weak or template websites.
problem: Consumers increasingly ask assistants to 'find and book' local help. Agents can't get a price, slot or deposit from a local trade without a call, so trades are invisible to agent-driven demand. Reviews and SEO matter less than being machine-readable and bookable.
solution: Each business gets an agent endpoint: photo-to-quote with vision models, service area and rules (minimum job, blackout dates), live slot holds, and a payment link for the deposit. It is exposed through structured data, an OpenAPI or MCP interface, and registered with agent platforms and directories. Owners set guardrails and approve borderline quotes by text.
why_now: Consumer agents and agentic-commerce protocols emerged in 2025-26 (prior knowledge), vision models can price photo-priceable jobs, and 46% of small firms already use AI, so owners are open to the concept.
revenue_model: $49/month plus a 3-5% booking fee on agent-originated jobs.
non_obvious_insight: The next website is a callable endpoint, and the first vertical where agents can close is the one where jobs are priceable from photos. Scheduling incumbents hold the data but may not expose a public agent interface, so a neutral gateway can win a directory position.
first_30_days: Sign 20 operators in two photo-priceable verticals, publish their endpoints and test with the major assistants' agent modes plus manual concierge. Measure agent-originated bookings and quote accuracy.

title: EU Liable-Party-of-Record for AI Products
one_liner: The registered agent of the AI era: an insured EU entity that stands as authorised representative under the new Product Liability Directive and keeps clients' evidence court-ready.
customer: Non-EU makers (10-200 staff) of AI-enabled consumer hardware and apps, such as robot vacuums, wearables, AI toys, smart-home and e-mobility firmware, selling into the EU via Amazon, Shopify or retailers.
problem: From 9 Dec 2026 software and AI count as 'products' under Directive 2024/2853. Courts can order disclosure of evidence, a defendant who stonewalls faces a presumption of defect, and liability cascades to importers, authorised representatives and fulfilment providers when no EU manufacturer exists. Small non-EU firms have no solvent EU counterparty, no organised technical file, and no cover. Marketplaces and logistics partners will start demanding all three.
solution: A fixed-fee service with four parts. (1) An EU entity acting as authorised representative and liable operator of record. (2) A 'disclosure-ready dossier': model and version registry, safety case, incident and OTA-update logs, and retention rules, collected through simple exports so a court order can be met in days. (3) EU-language complaint and defect intake plus recall coordination. (4) A bundled PLD policy through a fronting carrier or MGA, priced lower because the dossier removes unknowns.
why_now: The transposition deadline is 9 Dec 2026, about ten weeks away, and products placed on the market after it fall under the new regime. Only a minority of member states have finished transposing, so uncertainty peaks now. The December 2024 GPSR rule created a wave of paid 'EU responsible person' services, which shows small sellers buy this kind of compliance. Carriers filing broad AI exclusions (AIG, Berkley, Great American, ISO CG 40 47/48) push AI firms toward affirmative cover.
revenue_model: $1.5k-6k per month per client by risk tier, a $5-15k onboarding fee for the dossier, 10-15% commission on the bundled policy, and incident-response retainers. 40 clients at about $3k per month is roughly $1.4M ARR.
non_obvious_insight: The PLD creates an evidence-access war (disclosure orders plus presumptions of defect), and small firms lose it by default because they cannot produce coherent records. What clients buy is not legal advice but a solvent, present EU party who can hand a court a clean file. Demand will arrive through the distribution chain first, because retailers and marketplaces will impose it by contract before any regulator enforces it.
first_30_days: Partner with an EU product-liability law firm (NL, IE or DE) for the entity and an opinion letter. Publish a 10-page 'PLD readiness for AI hardware' guide. Pitch it to GPSR-rep leads, hardware accelerator alumni and Amazon/Shopify hardware sellers. Sign 5 founding clients at $1k per month. Get one European MGA or Lloyd's coverholder to quote the bundled policy.

title: Supply-House-Branded Back Office for Tiny Shops
one_liner: White-label quote, invoice, parts-pricing and trade-credit software delivered to solo-to-5-tech shops through their local independent supply house counter.
customer: Independent plumbing, HVAC, electrical and roofing supply houses and regional distributors squeezed by Home Depot (SRS, GMS, Mingledorff's) and Lowe's (FBM, Artisan). End users are their trade account holders.
problem: ServiceTitan fell about 26% after Q2 on slowing GTV, softer HVAC leads and a delay on exteriors, and expects only about 700 locations on its agentic tier. Most tiny shops have no operations layer and will not buy software cold, since CAC is brutal and churn high. Independent distributors are losing pro accounts to big-box integration and need a reason for contractors to stay.
solution: A private-label 'contractor OS' under the distributor's brand. Quotes are built from the distributor's live price book, invoices are text-to-pay, job notes and callbacks are tracked, truck stock reorders route to the counter, and net-30 parts credit is bundled. Counter staff onboard shops in person. It is free with a trade account, and the distributor pays per active shop.
why_now: Home Depot bought Mingledorff's in May 2026 on top of SRS and GMS, and Lowe's bought FBM for $8.8B. Independents' backs are against the wall. ServiceTitan's drop and deprioritization of exteriors leave small shops ignored. LLM-assisted development makes a lightweight tool cheap to build.
revenue_model: $30-60 per active shop per month paid by the distributor, or 0.25-0.5% of the shop's parts spend. Add payments interchange share and parts-financing spread.
non_obvious_insight: Vertical software wins on distribution. The supply house counter is the one place every tiny shop shows up every week, and distributors have both a strategic reason (defense against big-box) and a budget to pay for stickiness. Contractors will adopt anything that makes parts pricing and credit easier.
first_30_days: Sign two independent supply houses through buying-group contacts. Build an MVP on price-book CSV upload, SMS quotes and Stripe. Pilot with 20 shops per distributor and measure parts spend lift per shop.

title: Certified Coder Audit Pods for Autonomous Coding
one_liner: Displaced medical coders, organised as credentialed audit pods, provide the sampled human sign-off that lets hospitals trust autonomous coding AI to submit claims.
customer: Autonomous medical-coding vendors who need a human audit layer to close hospital deals, hospital revenue-cycle compliance leaders and physician groups. Pricing is $1.5-4 per audited chart or $15-40k a month per pod.
problem: Coding is a highly exposed white-collar job, and coders are being cut as autonomous coding reaches production. But billing compliance (False Claims Act exposure, payer and RAC audits) needs accountable, credentialed review. Vendors' own audit teams are thin or offshore and unlicensed.
solution: Pods of 5-10 CPC/CCS-certified ex-coders with a lead auditor, receiving risk-stratified samples of AI-coded charts via API. They provide error-taxonomy dashboards, monthly compliance attestations, feedback loops that retrain the model and contractual accuracy thresholds.
why_now: Autonomous coding moved into production in 2025-26, the coder job pool is shrinking, payers are using AI audits themselves and hospital margins are under pressure.
revenue_model: Per-chart fees or pod retainers at 45-55% gross margin, plus premium attestation packages.
non_obvious_insight: Full automation in healthcare billing stalls at the accountability signature, and the people displaced are the ones who can provide it. The human role shifts from doing to auditing a 5-10% sample, which is recurring compliance spend rather than labor cost. The audit data is also valuable training data for the vendor.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 laid-off certified coders through AAPC and AHIMA forums. Pitch 5 autonomous-coding startups a pilot: audit 1,000 charts at about $2 each with a written accuracy report. Sign one as a design partner.

title: Yes-in-God's-Backyard Deal Desk for Congregations
one_liner: A fixed-fee service that tells a shrinking congregation and its denomination what its land can legally become (by-right housing, ground lease, sale, merger), then runs the governance, title and buyer process.
customer: Regional denominational bodies (presbyteries, dioceses, Methodist conferences, Lutheran synods, synagogue federations) and boards of congregations with 50-250 members that hold a large building and lot they cannot afford to maintain. Secondary payers are affordable-housing developers and community land trusts that need sites.
problem: Per the briefing, only 33% of Americans attend monthly, Christian share has plateaued near 62%, and 18-24-year-olds are only 46% Christian, so many congregations sit on oversized buildings whose upkeep drains endowments. Selling is legally tangled: denominational trust clauses and canon-law approval thresholds, donor-restricted funds and cemeteries, state attorney-general notice for charitable assets, historic designation, and zoning. Lay boards typically wait for a crisis and then accept the first offer, usually an investor or another church. Meanwhile housing-shortage politics have produced by-right housing on religious land laws (California SB 4 took effect in 2024, with similar bills in other states, verify list), so the land may be worth multiples of the building, but few boards know it.
solution: Lead with a $1,500-3,000 'Land Options Report' covering parcel and zoning analysis under the state's faith-land housing law, likely unit yield, estimated residual land value against as-is sale, a title and restriction checklist, and a governance map of who must approve (trust clause, canon law, AG notice). Then sell a fixed-fee 'Transition Package': sequenced legal steps, member-vote scripts and communications, an RFP to pre-qualified faith-friendly developers (ground lease with a worship-space carve-out, so the congregation keeps a chapel and gets rent), and closing management. The report is automated with county parcel data plus LLM extraction of zoning code, reviewed by a real-estate/nonprofit attorney.
why_now: Pew's 2025 finding that decline has leveled but the generational gap is steep (briefing) means closures will keep coming for years. By-right faith-land housing laws are new (California SB 4 effective 2024, more states 2025-26, verify) and few boards know they exist. Cheap parcel data and LLM zoning-code reading make a $1,500 report profitable, where it used to need a $15k consultant.
revenue_model: Report fee of $1.5-3k, paid by congregations or as a bulk judicatory contract of $25-60k per year. Transition package at a fixed $15-40k or 1.5-3% of transaction value. Developer-side site-sourcing retainer or finder's fee, structured around broker-licensing rules.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not money or developers but a governance process a lay board can survive: each closure has 4-6 approval gates and any one can veto it. The value sits in a pre-mapped approval path for each denomination's polity. Under by-right housing, the residual land value often exceeds the building's as-is price, so the congregation that thinks it must close can instead become a landlord with a rent-paying chapel. Church brokers and developers each see only half of this.
first_30_days: Choose one state with a faith-land housing law and one denomination whose polity is well documented. Offer free Land Options Reports to 10 congregations referred by a regional official, in exchange for case-study rights and a $500 deposit. Hire a part-time real-estate/nonprofit attorney, assemble county GIS and zoning data, and pre-qualify 3 developers. Aim for 3-5 paid reports and one transition engagement within six months.

title: Book-Not-Shop Roll-Up of Retiring Machine Shops
one_liner: Buy retiring shops' customer books, programs and drawings on earn-outs, then migrate the work to a partner network.
customer: Owners of 5-40 person machine shops aged 60+ who want a clean exit. The buyer's customers keep their supply.
problem: About 60% of US manufacturing firms have owners aged 55+, about 150k small and mid-size firms are near retirement, and customers often leave when the owner retires (per American Machinist and MMS). MMS admits no dataset exists. Existing buyers such as Compass Precision buy whole shops with real estate, iron and payroll, which is capital-heavy and risky.
solution: Buy only the customer relationships, drawings, programs, fixtures and quality records for about 1-1.5x annual gross profit, paid mostly as an earn-out on retained revenue over 24-36 months. The owner runs a transition site for 6-12 months. Work then moves to 3-5 partner shops that have spare capacity. Equipment is auctioned or leased. AI digitizes quote history and setup sheets.
why_now: The retirement wave is under way and PMI at 55.6 (highest since May 2022) keeps demand steady. PE roll-ups have proven that a market exists, and a capital-light structure fits smaller teams.
revenue_model: 15-25% gross margin on migrated work. Slotting fees from partner shops. Deal capital is $250-750k per deal, mostly as earn-out.
non_obvious_insight: The asset is customer trust and tacit programs, not buildings or machines. An earn-out tied to retained revenue makes both sides fight the main failure mode of roll-ups, which is customer attrition.
first_30_days: Build a list of 300 target shops from state registries, LinkedIn and outreach. Sign three LOIs on owner-friendly terms. Line up three partner shops with capacity. Raise a $1M search-fund-style pool or use SBA financing.

title: Valet Keys for Delegated Browser Sessions
one_liner: An enforcement layer that lets an agent act inside your logged-in bank, airline or supplier portal, but only within per-site limits such as read-only here and a spend cap there.
customer: Enterprise finance-ops, revenue-cycle and logistics teams running browser agents on portals with no API (20-500 seats), followed by builders of prosumer browser agents who need a safety story.
problem: Insiders are building agent identity (OAuth for agents), but most delegated work rides on cookies in sites with no API. The agent inherits the user's full session. Browsers offer no primitive for a user to see, scope or withdraw an agent's access. If the user is legally the one who accessed the site, as the Ninth Circuit reasoned, the user owns everything the agent does with that session.
solution: A browser extension plus enforcement proxy with per-site policy packs that classify actions (view, draft, submit, pay, change credentials) using URL, DOM and network patterns. Irreversible actions are denied by default, with spend and count caps, step-up approval and signed action receipts. Ship maintained packs for the top 200 enterprise portals (payer, carrier, marketplace seller-center and bank portals) and update them as sites change.
why_now: Browser agents went mainstream in 2026, and about 21,600 OpenClaw instances were found exposed. Machine identities outnumber humans roughly 109 to 1, and the agent-equals-user doctrine puts liability on the delegating user.
revenue_model: $15-40 per seat per month for enterprises, policy-pack subscriptions, and a per-session API price for agent vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The missing primitive is a valet key (parks the car, cannot open the trunk) for sessions. The moat is the maintained per-site action taxonomy, which is tedious, unglamorous and hard to copy.
first_30_days: Find one revenue-cycle or logistics ops team already using browser agents and build read-only plus draft-only policy packs for the 5 portals they use. Run a $2k/month pilot and log blocked actions as proof of value.

title: Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure
one_liner: A daily feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements to show who is quietly assembling land for data centers, solar and transmission weeks before anyone announces it.
customer: Competing data center, solar, storage and transmission developers' land teams and site-selection consultants; utility and co-op large-load planners; infrastructure and energy funds buying alternative data; and county economic development and planning offices wanting defensive visibility.
problem: Land assembly is a race, and the first public trace is a short memorandum of option, lease or easement recorded at the county. Nobody watches those at scale. The assessor doesn't reflect an unexercised option. The clerk's document-type field is a dropdown chosen by a data-entry clerk, so big deals hide under 'Other', 'Miscellaneous' or 'Agreement'. Developers find out about a competitor's 6,000 acres months late, counties learn from a leaked newspaper story, and everyone pays landmen $300-$600 a day to sit in vaults.
solution: Ingest recorded instruments from county portals and bulk feeds in target corridors. Classify by reading the full image, not the clerk's label. Cluster by grantee, signatory, notary, return-to law firm and mailing address to unmask LLC families. Flag assembly events, such as N option memos within X miles or easement clusters along a line that imply transmission or pipeline. Deliver alerts, a map, and parcel-level chain-of-title and existing-easement packets on demand, with a human landman reviewing the hard ones.
why_now: The 2025-2026 large-load land rush is real: options in Hallam, Nebraska are reportedly worth tens of thousands of dollars an acre, and Hill County, Texas land appraised near $7,100 an acre has been offered about $100,000 an acre. Options are documented only by memoranda under NDA. FinCEN's 2025 decision to exempt domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision finally reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $2k-$8k/month per regional developer or utility seat, $750-$2,000 per tract title packet, and $50k-$150k/year alt-data licenses for funds. Optional revenue share or free access for counties that provide bulk feeds.
non_obvious_insight: The return-to address and notary on a recorded memorandum are the fingerprint of the developer's counsel, and they reveal an assembly weeks before a rezoning hearing. The mislabeled document-type field is why nobody has done this with generic data vendors. Landmen are the recorder's best regulars and know exactly which counties are hot, which makes them the cheapest ground-truth labelers and first customers.
first_30_days: Choose two counties with a rumored project, pull 24 months of instruments, and build the classifier and clustering. Deliver a 'who is assembling where' memo free to 10 site-selection consultants and land brokers, then convert two into $3k-$5k pilots. Check each state's bulk-data commercial-use rules and offer the counties access to the same maps.

title: Reefer Claim Vault for Small Carriers
one_liner: An always-on evidence recorder that captures the proof that decides cargo claims, giving small carriers and their cargo insurers a one-click defense packet.
customer: Small reefer and dry-van carriers (1 to 50 trucks), especially produce and protein lanes, and the cargo-insurance agencies and MGAs that write them. Brokers needing reefer-specific carrier diligence are a secondary buyer.
problem: Small carriers lose or pay $5k to $60k cargo claims not because they were at fault but because they can't prove it. Pre-cool temperature, setpoint, continuous versus cycle-sentry mode, who loaded and counted, and seal integrity all decide a Carmack claim, and the evidence is usually never captured or gets overwritten on the reefer unit. After a claim, the cargo insurer raises rates or cancels. Post-Montgomery, reefer-specific vetting is also becoming a standard-of-care question for brokers.
solution: A driver app with a 90-second guided pickup ritual: photo of the empty trailer floor and reefer display, pre-cool temp, setpoint and mode, seal photo before the forklift touches it, an OCR check of the BOL that flags a missing 'SL&C' (shipper load and count) notation, seal number or temp instructions, and a Bluetooth probe reading of product temperature at load. It pulls continuous temperature records from reefer telematics (Thermo King, Carrier) or a $30 BLE data logger and hash-timestamps everything. When a claim lands, it generates a Carmack-structured defense packet in one click. Insurers get aggregate loss-prevention scoring by carrier.
why_now: The 2026 Montgomery ruling has brokers and insurers paying attention to reefer diligence. Cargo losses and theft are up sharply (Verisk CargoNet Q2 2026 losses of $304.6M). Vision AI makes BOL and photo checking cheap, and reefer telematics APIs and cheap Bluetooth loggers have matured.
revenue_model: $25 to $40 per truck per month for carriers. MGAs and agencies pay $10 per truck per month or fund the subscription in exchange for loss-ratio improvement and premium credits. A $150 flat fee per claim-defense packet for non-subscribers as a low-friction entry.
non_obvious_insight: Claims are decided by paper nobody produced in the sixty seconds when it mattered. Every veteran knows the ritual: write SL&C on the BOL, photograph the seal before anyone touches the door, snap the pre-cool, and download the reefer unit before it rolls over. Nobody does it consistently because nobody reminds them at the dock. Insurers see the losses but not the cause, so they will pay to change driver behavior at the moment of pickup.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 small cargo-insurance agencies that specialize in trucking. Recruit 20 reefer carriers hauling produce (Fresno to Nogales, Yakima, Salinas). Give them a free 30-day pilot plus the BLE logger at cost. Build a PWA using photo capture and Claude vision for BOL checks. Track claim outcomes on pilot trucks versus a control group to build the insurer's business case.

title: AI Coverage Buy-Back Packs for Insurance Agents
one_liner: An intake that turns a small business's AI usage into an underwriter-ready 'AI use and guardrails' package so its insurer will restore the coverage it just excluded.
customer: Independent insurance agencies and brokerages that serve SMBs, who pay per client pack or a monthly agency subscription. Their clients are marketing agencies, law and accounting firms, clinics, staffing firms and e-commerce brands that use AI heavily.
problem: ISO endorsements CG 40 47 and CG 40 48 took effect in January 2026 and let carriers exclude generative-AI-related bodily injury, property damage and advertising injury from standard general liability policies. Reporting says Chubb, Travelers and Berkshire Hathaway got state approvals, and more than 80% of such requests were approved. Absolute AI exclusions are also appearing on D&O and E&O policies, including for 'allegedly inadequate AI governance'. About 74% of small businesses already use AI tools, and agents cannot tell clients what evidence underwriters will accept.
solution: A 15-minute intake, plus an optional SSO or browser scan, inventories the client's AI tools. It maps each use (customer chatbot, AI-generated ads, AI hiring screens, AI note-takers with client data) to the coverage lines it touches. It then produces: (1) a coverage-gap report that flags CG 40 47/48 and absolute AI exclusions in the current policy, (2) an underwriter-ready AI use and guardrails statement with a human-review log and vendor list, and (3) a quote-request package aimed at markets that sell affirmative AI coverage or buy-backs. Every pack also gives the agent a talk track for the renewal meeting.
why_now: The exclusions have been in effect since January 2026 and are now hitting renewals. Search interest is rising in the underlying concepts: Exploding Topics shows AI Guardrails +8,400%, Responsible AI +3,600% and Cyber Insurance +763%. Colorado's AI Act, delayed to Jan 1, 2027, and Illinois HB 3773 (in effect Jan 1, 2026) add employer-side documentation duties that the same pack can reuse.
revenue_model: $149-$299 per client pack, or $199-$499/month per agency for unlimited packs plus renewal reminders. Later: a referral or placement fee from managing general agents and carriers that write AI buy-backs, and a co-branded version sold through carrier appointment programs.
non_obvious_insight: The evidence standard does not exist yet. Law firm analyses of the exclusions note they 'stop short of prescribing specific governance standards insurers will accept' (https://www.lathropgpm.com/insights/the-ai-coverage-gap-what-new-insurance-exclusions-mean-for-your-business/) and describe fragmenting coverage across GL, D&O, E&O and EPLI (https://www.fenwick.com/insights/publications/end-silent-ai-emerging-ai-exclusions-coverage-fragmentation-and-practical-implications). Whichever evidence format two or three underwriters or MGAs accept first will become the SOC 2 of AI coverage. Agents, not the businesses themselves, are the right buyer because they lose commission if a client goes bare. Cyber-insurance search interest is up 763% and AI Guardrails up 8,400% (https://explodingtopics.com/finance-topics, https://explodingtopics.com/blog/trending-topics), which shows SMBs are already looking for this without a product to buy.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the intake form and PDF generator, and interview 15 independent agents (local IIABA and Big I chapters, LinkedIn) about how renewals with AI exclusions are being handled. Days 11-20: run free packs for each agent's five most AI-heavy clients, and ask two MGA underwriters whether the format is acceptable. Days 21-30: start charging $149 per pack. Target 5 agencies at $199/month and post 'we got X's AI coverage bought back' cases from the pilots.

title: Quality-of-Earnings Audits for Robot Fleets
one_liner: A finance-native auditor that verifies deployed units, productive hours, teleoperation share and revenue per robot for the lenders, lessors and investors underwriting robot, AV and drone fleets.
customer: Lenders, equipment lessors, SPAC sponsors, growth funds and acquirers underwriting robotics, AV and drone companies. Second wave: insurers of AV trucks and warehouse robots, and investors in robot-as-a-service lease pools.
problem: Robotics valuations run on self-reported fleet metrics. Agility reported $1.8M of 2025 revenue against a $2.5B SPAC. Maven raised $100M with about 8 robots deployed. Serve booked about $1.3k of revenue per robot. Figure reports about 740 robots against about 600 employees. 1X NEO's early demos were largely teleoperated. Nobody audits 'deployed' vs 'productive' vs 'autonomous' vs 'paid'. AV insurers price 'slightly above' human trucks on the unknown, and lessors cannot underwrite $499-$600/mo robot leases blind.
solution: A boutique assurance firm. Under NDA it gets read-only telemetry, remote-assist logs and billing, and visits sites. It produces a signed Fleet QoE report with standard metrics: units deployed vs productive hours, human interventions per robot-hour, revenue and margin per unit, safety events, uptime and maintenance cost, and contract quality. Later, publish a standard 'Fleet Passport' for covenant reporting.
why_now: About 22,000 humanoids shipped in H1 2026. Unitree IPO'd in Aug 2026. Agility is going public via SPAC. Figure plans a $600/mo lease. Skild ($14B) and Physical Intelligence ($11B) are priced for perfection. Leasing and asset-backed structures for robots are being invented now, and capital allocators need evidence, not demos.
revenue_model: $40k-$120k per diligence engagement, buyer-paid. $10k-$30k per year of continuous covenant monitoring for lenders and lessors. An anonymized benchmark data license to insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The metric that decides whether a robotics company is a software business or a labor-arbitrage business, hidden human-intervention hours per robot-hour, is invisible to the buyer. Capital allocators, not vendors, must be the payer, because vendor-paid attestation fails (Trustpilot was fined for selling to those it rates). An ex-assurance plus ex-robotics team beats a technical certifier.
first_30_days: Write a 40-item data request and an intervention-hour analysis template. Recruit an ex-Big-4 assurance lead and one robotics ops engineer. Offer two free pilot audits to a debt fund or equipment lessor with a robot deal in progress. Publish an anonymized 'what to ask a robotics CEO' metrics guide. Aim for one paid engagement letter within 60-90 days.

title: Closed-School Science Labs Shipped to African Schools
one_liner: Take decommissioned lab benches, microscopes, fume hoods and Chromebooks from US schools being closed, refurbish them into container-sized lab packages with a practical-exam curriculum, and sell them to private secondary schools in East and West Africa.
customer: Buyers are private and faith-based secondary school networks in Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria and Ghana, paying $8-15k per lab package. Sellers are US districts, charters and private schools that are closing and want fast, lawful disposal at low cost.
problem: More than 1,000 US public schools closed in 2025-26. Chicago alone has 135k empty seats, and Portland, Minneapolis and Albuquerque are queued behind it. Districts dispose of equipment through slow public-surplus auctions that recover pennies. Meanwhile African private schools running on tiny per-student budgets cannot afford lab equipment, even though national practical exams and newer competency-based curricula require it. A new lab costs $30-50k and takes months to import.
solution: Inventory soon-to-close buildings and remove complete science rooms, robotics kits, libraries and tested Chromebooks (with NIST-grade data wipes and export of working goods only). Bundle them into a 40-foot container with local installation, a practical-exam curriculum (matched to Kenyan, Nigerian or Ghanaian exam boards), a one-day teacher orientation, and a small annual refill of consumables. The district gets a disposal certificate and a possible donation receipt.
why_now: Closures are at a four-year high, so supply is predictable and geographically concentrated. The AI memory crunch, with memory now 30-40% of a device's bill of materials, has raised new-device prices and made used Chromebooks valuable. Distributed solar and batteries mean African schools can now run lab equipment and computers. As I understand it, Kenya's first competency-based senior-school cohort (2026) requires STEM practicals many schools cannot deliver.
revenue_model: Lab packages sell at $9-14k against a landed cost of $5-6k. A curriculum and refill subscription adds $600 per school per year. Districts pay a $1-3k decommissioning fee per closure in place of an auction consignment fee, or grant surplus title for free.
non_obvious_insight: A closing school is a fully assembled, curriculum-matched capital asset that public procurement can only sell by the pound, while the same asset is the binding constraint on practical-exam pass rates in low-fee African schools. The margin is in the bundle of equipment, practical curriculum and teacher orientation, not in the equipment, and that bundle is exactly what charity donation programs do not offer.
first_30_days: Pick one district and walk three soon-to-close buildings. Offer free removal of the first 10 science rooms in exchange for title to the equipment. Get letters of intent and 30% deposits from two or three African private-school owners through diaspora, church or school-association networks. Ship one container of two labs plus 200 tested Chromebooks. Line up an export broker and a data-wipe vendor before touching anything.

title: Sleep-Apnea-to-GLP-1 Pathway for DME Suppliers
one_liner: A co-management service that lets sleep labs and CPAP suppliers prescribe, retest and retain patients as they lose weight.
customer: Independent sleep centers, home-sleep-test companies and DME suppliers whose profit engine is CPAP resupply.
problem: Zepbound was approved for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity on Dec 20, 2024, and Part D can cover it for OSA. As weight falls, patients drop CPAP without a retest or re-titration, and the DME loses resupply revenue and the patient. Sleep clinics have no pathway for prescribing or co-managing a drug.
solution: Baseline and 3/6/12-month home sleep tests, benefits verification and prior authorization for Zepbound-for-OSA, a nutrition and muscle plan, auto-CPAP pressure re-titration from device data, and a 'retest before you quit CPAP' protocol. DMEs keep the supply relationship where still needed.
why_now: The OSA indication now has Medicare and commercial coverage routes, and cash pricing is falling, so patient demand is arriving at sleep clinics without a pathway. DMEs see the threat and hold the patient data (CPAP usage) needed to co-manage.
revenue_model: $15-30 per patient per month to the DME or sleep center, or a share of retained resupply, plus per-test fees.
non_obvious_insight: The DME supplier looks like the loser but is the natural gatekeeper: it has adherence data, patient trust and a recurring billing relationship, and it will pay to convert lost resupply into a managed weight-and-airway program.
first_30_days: Approach 5 regional DMEs or sleep centers. Pilot on 100 CPAP patients with BMI of 30 or more and AHI of 15 or more. Measure PA success, retest rate and retained resupply.

title: Prospecting for Brackish Aquifers Like Gold
one_liner: A water-exploration company that maps, options and permits high-yield brackish and fresh aquifers before developers need them, then sells or leases 'water-ready' sites and supply.
customer: Data-center developers, small towns and rural districts, ranchers and industrial parks needing 1-5 MGD of defensible supply. Buyers pay for studies, and later for site options and supply contracts.
problem: About 1,800 ERCOT projects are held, and water is the new gating item. Siting decisions are still made on power and fiber first, and water studies come late from generalist consultants. Groundwater in Texas is private property under the rule of capture subject to local district rules (my understanding), so early options on proven supply are valuable, yet almost nobody is exploring for water the way miners explore for minerals.
solution: Use public airborne-electromagnetic surveys, well logs and machine learning to map the probability of high-yield brackish aquifers. Option land and water rights, drill test wells, obtain production permits, and pair with a treatment partner. Sell paid site reports first, then options and long-term supply.
why_now: Drone-borne electromagnetic surveys are getting cheap, brackish desalination costs are falling, and regulators are blocking new load without a proven water plan.
revenue_model: $15-75k paid site studies, drilling programs on cost-plus or success fee, and $1-5M site-option or supply sales.
non_obvious_insight: Water rights are the new mineral rights. The geophysics is becoming a commodity, but the permitting playbook and early option positions are not.
first_30_days: Sell five 'water-ready screening' reports at $15-25k to developers in the ERCOT queue and to towns, using public data only. Line up a drilling partner and identify two parcels near transmission with promising brackish aquifers to option.

title: Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions
one_liner: A payoff-desk plug-in that finds the unearned GAP and service-contract refunds the moment a member pays off, and applies unearned add-on credits in repossession deficiencies. It goes through lenders, not SEO, so it reaches the borrowers the consumer refund sites can't.
customer: Credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and collections departments). The lender pays a small SaaS fee or takes a share of recovered money. Second wedge: consumer bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid, at $99 per deficiency audit.
problem: When a borrower pays off early, trades in, or has the car totaled or repossessed, they are owed the unearned pro-rata part of GAP, service contracts and other financed add-ons. Refunds are not automatic. Not the dealer, not the lender and not the administrator processes them, and consumer-refund sites exist because so few people claim. The incentives point the wrong way. The dealer suffers a commission chargeback, so it stalls. The administrator profits from non-cancellation. The lender never owned the product. The borrower doesn't know. In repossession, unearned add-on credits should reduce the deficiency the borrower is sued for, and they rarely appear on deficiency notices. Roughly 3M repossessions a year and subprime 60+ day delinquency at a 32-year record of 6.9% in January 2026 make this a very large pool of missed money.
solution: Ingest the closed-loan document image or loan tape, read the itemized products and financed amounts from the retail installment contract, and match each to its administrator. Compute the pro-rata or earned-basis refund by state rule (New Jersey, for example, requires an automatic refund within 60 days). Auto-generate the cancellation packet with the lender's payoff letter, odometer statement, signature or letter of authority, and the state statute citation, then track it to payment. Stalled cases escalate to the state insurance department with a complaint file. The moat is a database of roughly 60 administrators' actual cancellation requirements and response behavior, plus the 50-state rule set. The repossession product reconciles deficiency notices against the same data and outputs an attorney-ready exhibit.
why_now: Record delinquencies and about 3M repossessions a year, roughly 84-month loans with about 30% of trade-ins underwater, and long terms mean most loans die early and carry stacked add-ons. Credit unions are under member-experience and fee-optics pressure, and California's SB 766 now requires dealers to keep refund and cancellation records. LLMs can finally read messy contract images and cancellation forms cheaply enough to run at scale.
revenue_model: Credit union pays $3 to $6 per payoff processed, or 20 to 30% of recovered money with no upfront fee. Attorneys pay $99 per deficiency audit or a $499 per month subscription. Later, sell aggregated administrator refund-speed benchmarks to dealer groups and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The consumer refund sites that exist all have the same weakness: they wait for the borrower to show up. The one moment every party knows the loan ended is the payoff, and the lender's payoff desk is the only place that sees all of them. The refund itself comes from the administrator's pool, and the dealer's chargeback is a fight between the dealer and the administrator. The borrower's claim doesn't depend on the dealer cooperating, so the dealer stalling does not need to hold up the refund.
first_30_days: Build the administrator playbook for the 20 largest GAP and service-contract administrators and the 10 highest-population states. Offer 3 credit unions a free retrospective audit of 500 payoffs from the last 12 months and show them the dollar total of unclaimed refunds. Take a 30% success fee on live recoveries. Simultaneously give 5 consumer bankruptcy attorneys the repossession deficiency audit free on their next 3 cases in return for case studies.

title: Data Center Deal Desk for Rural Counties
one_liner: An independent negotiating desk that gives county and township boards a benchmark of every comparable data-center abatement and community-benefit contract, a counter term sheet and a fiscal model, paid for by the developer's review escrow.
customer: County commissions, township boards, school boards and local economic-development authorities facing data-center proposals, plus state associations of counties and resident coalitions.
problem: Developers have negotiated dozens of deals and arrive with NDAs and shell LLCs. Counties have negotiated none, and commissioners vote on abatements they can't benchmark. Leverage disappears once approvals are granted. Terms on water use, noise, diesel backup hours, decommissioning bonds, grid-cost protection and clawbacks vary wildly.
solution: Parse every signed abatement, PILOT, host-community and large-load utility agreement obtainable (the Federation of American Scientists started collecting signed agreements in early 2026, and public records requests fill gaps) into a comparable clause database. Deliver a two-week Deal Review: where each term falls against the median and best deals, a counter term sheet, fiscal, water and power impact modeling, and a 'second chair' during meetings. Fees are typically recoverable from the applicant through a third-party review escrow.
why_now: The 2026 data-center land rush has local governments scrambling: most local ordinances and ballot measures tracked in 2026 passed, many deals sit behind NDAs, and counties from Texas to Ohio are tabling or denying abatements while others approve blind. LLMs make reading hundreds of messy contracts cheap. Incumbent consultants and county attorneys don't have a comparables dataset.
revenue_model: $12k to $40k per deal review (billed to the developer's review escrow where the county allows it), annual data license for state county associations ($30k to $100k) and, later, a pre-vetted 'fast-lane' term sheet that developers pay to use.
non_obvious_insight: Information asymmetry, not law, is the county's problem, and the cheapest fix is a set of comparables. Commissioners also fear being first or being fleeced, so 'we asked for what the median county got' gives political cover. Charging the applicant through the review escrow means the buyer, a cash-strapped county, doesn't need a budget line.
first_30_days: Collect 100 signed agreements from the FAS repository, Texas Chapter 312 filings and records requests, and code them into a comparison table. Publish free state scorecards. Email commissioners in counties with pending abatement votes and offer a $5k rapid clause redline, asking the county to request that the developer pay under its review-fee ordinance.

title: Vaults After Banks
one_liner: Buy or lease closed bank branches with intact vaults and reopen them as private safe-deposit clubs for the people banks are abandoning.
customer: Crypto self-custodians storing seed-phrase backups, families doing estate planning, small collectors and small businesses. Referral channels are estate attorneys and financial advisors. Boxes run $150-900/yr.
problem: Big banks are exiting safe-deposit service. JPMorgan is reported to be leaving the business, and Santander and Capital One have stopped new boxes. Large boxes have multi-year waitlists in cities. Storing seed phrases or a will at home is risky, and a bank box has a known weakness: heirs can't get in without a court process.
solution: Acquire or lease shuttered branches whose UL-rated vaults and box banks are already installed. Sunk-cost vaults are nearly worthless to a seller and costly to build new. Add modern access control (biometrics plus dual-key, video, private viewing booths) and insurance. Build a strong KYC and lawful-process program from day one, without inventorying box contents. Then differentiate with a sealed 'Legacy Envelope': tamper-evident, chain-of-custody logged, and released to named heirs through an attorney-verified protocol. Add a notary and witness room for signing estate documents on site.
why_now: Bank exits are accelerating through 2025-26, and branch closures keep feeding the market with sale-ready vault buildings. Self-custodied crypto has gone mainstream, and holders are worried about physical coercion. Independent operators like BlueVault report growing demand, so the model is proven but far from saturated outside a few metros.
revenue_model: Annual box rent ($120-900 by size). One-time onboarding fee. Legacy Envelope release plans ($60/yr plus $250 on release). Hourly notary and witness room. Attorney and advisor referral fees. A 1,500-box vault at about 70% fill and $300 average is roughly $315k/yr against a building that can cost $250-500k.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is trust and the legal chain of custody after death, not the steel. Banks leave because a box earns little against corporate overhead, but a one-branch boutique with a lawyer-drafted custody agreement is profitable. The US Private Vaults FBI seizure in 2021 shows the failure mode, so the winning brand is 'privacy plus compliance', never 'no questions asked'.
first_30_days: Pull 20 recently closed branches from LoopNet and bank real-estate-owned lists and shortlist the ones with intact vaults and box banks. Get a vault-contractor inspection and an insurance quote. Have a lawyer draft the custody agreement and Legacy Envelope protocol. Open a waitlist with $100 refundable founding-member deposits, targeting 300 members through crypto meetups and estate-attorney networks before signing a lease.

title: Guild-Issued Credentials That Beat Free Badges
one_liner: Turn illustrator, photographer, translator and indie-label associations into verifiers that issue portable 'real working creator' credentials.
customer: Trade associations, unions and guilds with 1,000-50,000 members who need visible AI-era member value. Second-side buyers are contests, publishers, agencies and brands that want to check a creator quickly.
problem: Insiders assume a universal proof-of-personhood is needed, like World's iris scans or platform badges. But Spotify says over 99% of artists listeners search for are already verified, so a free badge says nothing about who is a working professional. The brief flags that a paid credential must beat the free native one, and it cannot do so on 'is human' alone.
solution: A white-label service where the guild verifies members using its own dues records and portfolio review, and we issue portable credentials. These are W3C verifiable credentials, Bluesky trusted-verifier labels, a signed .well-known file for members' websites and an embeddable badge. A lookup API lets buyers and contest platforms verify membership and standing. Guilds also get a public directory.
why_now: Org-issued verification became a working pattern on Bluesky in 2025, and TikTok joining C2PA in Jul 2026 shows provenance moving to the mainstream. Guild members are demanding concrete AI-era protection, and platform badges are free and universal, so they cannot signal professional standing.
revenue_model: Association license of $5-25k/year, $1-3 per member per year for issuance, and lookup fees for enterprise buyers such as contests and agencies.
non_obvious_insight: The value of verification comes from the stakes and scarcity of the issuer, not from cryptography. Guilds already own the membership record and the trust, and a platform that gives everyone a badge cannot compete with that.
first_30_days: Pitch 20 mid-size associations with a one-page offer: a 3-week pilot of 100 verified members on Bluesky and their own websites. Charge a $2-5k pilot fee, and aim to have one association make it a renewal benefit.

title: Offline Brain for Talking Toys
one_liner: A sub-$20 on-device speech-and-language module that lets toys hold child-safe conversations with no cloud, no audio leaving the toy and parent-readable summaries on the parent's phone.
customer: Toy brands and ODMs, indie AI-toy startups and kids' IP licensors who fear cloud data liability.
problem: Cloud-based AI toys stream children's voices to servers, which the amended COPPA rule (biometrics, retention limits, separate opt-in for third-party sharing) makes risky. Brand exposure is rising after consumer tests and lawsuits. Toy makers lack model-safety teams, and per-conversation cloud costs collide with a one-time hardware sale.
solution: A reference design and software stack: kid-tuned speech recognition, a 1-4B-parameter model fine-tuned for age-banded personas and refusals, and text-to-speech on a $10-15 NPU chip. Safety-locked story and play modes, and Bluetooth summaries to a parent app. Licensed to ODMs, with dev kits for startups.
why_now: Small on-device models reached conversational quality in 2025-26 and cheap NPUs run them in real time, so the technology only just became feasible. Regulation turns cloud audio into a liability, and holiday 2026 is the first big AI-toy season.
revenue_model: $2-4 per unit licence, $299 dev kits, and paid NRE for custom personas.
non_obvious_insight: The cloud is both the risk and the cost. On-device removes marginal cost and turns COPPA from a burden into a marketing claim ('nothing leaves the toy'), fixing the broken subscription-for-hardware model.
first_30_days: Prototype on a Raspberry Pi 5 or RK3588 board with an off-the-shelf small model. Measure latency and accuracy on consented child speech. Demo to 15 indie toy makers on Kickstarter and Crowd Supply and to 2 ODMs. Aim for 2 paid dev-kit pilots with $5k NRE each.

title: Workup Cover: Insurance for Scan Findings
one_liner: A prepaid guarantee sold at checkout for $800-$1,000 whole-body MRIs and $949 cancer blood tests that covers the second read, the guideline triage and pre-priced follow-up when a scan finds something.
customer: Cash-pay screening buyers 45-70 (whole-body MRI, multi-cancer blood tests, coronary calcium, low-dose CT). First, people who already hold a frightening PDF; second, imaging centers and screening brands that want higher conversion and fewer angry customers; third, concierge doctors and employers.
problem: Screening has gotten cheap enough for the middle class (Function Health's Ezra scan lists at $999 or $799 for members, SimonMed at $899 promotional). The FDA advisory panel voted on September 23, 2026 to back Grail's Galleri blood test, and a new law lets Medicare cover such tests starting in 2028. But the tail is unpriced and unmanaged: in one large study about one in three whole-body MRI participants had an incidental finding and 62% of those biopsied had no malignancy, and the American College of Radiology does not recommend total-body MRI for average-risk adults. The follow-up (specialist visits, repeat imaging, biopsy) is stressful, uncoordinated and can run into the thousands.
solution: An add-on with three layers. (1) A subspecialty radiologist second read within 48 hours. (2) Guideline-based triage (Bosniak, TI-RADS, Fleischner, LI-RADS) that turns the majority of low-risk findings into 'do nothing or repeat in 12 months' with a written explanation. (3) A nurse navigator who books any needed follow-up at pre-negotiated cash prices and, once loss data exist, a financial cap on follow-up costs underwritten with a reinsurer or managing general agent. Phase 1 has no underwriting: sell 'Second Read and Triage' for $149 standalone; Phase 2 adds the guarantee.
why_now: Three things converged in 2025-26: scan prices fell below $1,000 through Function Health and others, the first FDA advisory-panel endorsement of a multi-cancer blood test arrived, and Medicare coverage is scheduled for 2028. Volume of consumer screening is climbing while incidental-finding anxiety is a top complaint in patient communities.
revenue_model: $149-249 attach fee at time of scan purchase (screening seller keeps 20-30% revenue share), $199 standalone second reads, and reinsured guarantee margin: most findings resolve with a read, so expected follow-up payout per member is a small fraction of the fee. Later: protocol licensing to health systems and imaging chains.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to mass preventive screening is not the price of the test but the unpriced tail. Pricing the tail like an extended warranty turns screening's biggest ethical objection (cascades of follow-up) into a product feature, and it lets cheap scans sell without the seller being blamed for the aftermath. A radiology-native underwriter also prices this risk better than a generic insurer.
first_30_days: Recruit three moonlighting subspecialty teleradiologists licensed in target states and one RN navigator. Set up secure image upload with an off-the-shelf DICOM-sharing platform. Launch a $149 'Scary PDF Second Read' in the patient communities around Prenuvo and Function, and sign referral agreements with two independent imaging centers selling $899 MRIs. Log every finding and outcome to price the guarantee. Target 100 second reads in 60 days.
